Leah and Claire, September 6, 2016 — first day of kindergarten, chalkboard held with both hands.

♡Family Today♡

Dunkirk was a success. The yard is done, the crew got home, and the paper is told the dinner was the best part. Thank you to Grandpa and Grandma for the meal and for putting up with all of us — that kind of hospitality is the whole reason anybody drives an hour each way. Today is quieter: 69 and partly sunny, with rain holding off until the small hours.
  • Sep 20Packers at Jets — Sunday, 1:00
  • Sep 26Harvest Moon, full at 12:48 p.m.
  • Sep 27Chargers at Buffalo — 1:00
  • Nov 3Election Day
Had a migraine? Say so in the group chat — the day and roughly when — and the paper will mark it on the Barograph. Enough entries and we will know what the glass does before one hits.

Outdoor window Open all day and into the evening. Showers arrive after one in the morning and settle in for tomorrow between seven and two — a quarter to half an inch. Nothing gets above 66 for the next week. Autumn is official Tuesday at 10:05 a.m. and the weather has already agreed. Pollen Ragweed high.

🍂The Turning🍂

Still no number for the three counties. The spotters out this far have not logged enough change to call it, which is where the third week of September usually sits.
Anyone who was raking in Dunkirk yesterday has a better read than the state does. First thing to go is the sumac on the shoulders, then the crowns of the red maples along the creek roads. Numbers as soon as the spotters file them; North Tonawanda usually peaks the last week of October.

☾The Almanac Sky☾

Past first quarter, 57 percent, now in Capricorn and setting at 12:18 a.m. It is up all evening, which is the good news; clouds thicken after midnight, which is the rest of it.
Sun 6:59a – 7:18p · 12h 19m · 3h 5m shorter than June 21
Next new moon Sat, Oct 10 · Harvest Moon Sat, Sep 26
Tonight Saturn rises in the east at 7:57. Jupiter comes up at 3:33 a.m. Three days to the equinox, Tuesday at 10:05 a.m.; daylight is down to twelve hours nineteen minutes and still falling three a day.
Aries
Mercury in Libra is still opposite Saturn in your sign, into a third day and now within two degrees. This is the aspect that makes an ordinary conversation feel heavier than it is. It is nearly exact — which means it is nearly over. Kaylani, Luka
Cancer
Mars at twenty-five degrees of Cancer holds its sextile to the Sun, the last few days of the most productive angle it makes all year. Mars leaves your sign within the week. Whatever you have been pushing, push it now. Gregg
Leo
Mercury in Libra runs sextile to Jupiter in your sign today — the aspect of the useful conversation, the one that opens a door without anyone planning it. Jupiter is in Leo until next summer; this is the kind of day it does its work. Leah, Tommy
Virgo
The Sun is at twenty-six degrees of Virgo, three days from leaving. Your season ends Tuesday morning with the equinox. A Virgo's instinct is to finish the list before the deadline; you have seventy-two hours and it is not a metaphor. Derek, Joanne
Scorpio
Venus in Scorpio is still square Pluto, and today the Moon in Capricorn runs sextile to Venus — a softer note inside a tense aspect. Translation: you will want something intensely and also be reasonable about it. Rare combination. Use it. Ariel, Claire, Garret

September 6, 2016 was a Tuesday, and the chalkboard in today's plate got held up for the camera the way they always do. Ten school years on. Somebody in this family is going to want that photo printed.

✶The National Wire✶

1

U.N. Mission Finds Evidence of U.S. War Crimes in Iran

A fact-finding report cites strikes on civilian sites in the seven-month war. The administration rejected the findings outright.

2

Congress Clears New Sanctions on Russia and Iran

The House approved the measure Wednesday; the Senate passed it last month. It is named for the late Lindsey Graham.

3

More Ships Hit in Hormuz as Gas Climbs

Iran struck additional vessels in the strait this week. Asked about pump prices, the president said they were not soaring.

4

World Leaders Arrive for the General Assembly

The U.N. session and Climate Week open in New York. Oxfam released a report calling global inequality an emergency.

☑The Ballot☑

The Governor's Race, and the Ads
Forty-five days. Hochul led Blakeman 49–39 in the August Siena poll of likely voters — a ten-point race, down from twenty in June. No Republican has won statewide in New York since Pataki in 2002. Blakeman, 70, is the Nassau County executive; Trump endorsed him after Elise Stefanik left the race. He is running on taxes, crime and utility bills, and blamed Hochul for energy costs at the State Fair in Syracuse last month.
The part that is genuinely new is how he is advertising. Blakeman's campaign has run a series of ads built with generative A.I. that fabricate Hochul's voice and likeness. In them the invented Hochul has robbed a bank, been offered drugs by a dealer, gambled taxpayer money alongside Mayor Mamdani, and — in one posted this month — gardened and rode bicycles with Mamdani while the two of them pitched “delusion pills” for the cost-of-living crisis. The voice is synthetic. The words were never said.
New York amended its election law to require that “materially deceptive” political material be labeled as A.I.-generated, with an exception for satire and parody. The state Democratic Party filed a complaint with the Board of Elections; a Washington Post review found that not all of the ads carry a disclosure. Blakeman invokes the satire clause. “People find it humorous. They like satire,” he said, and to critics calling the ads A.I. slop: “They should get a life. Comedy has been used in political campaigns from the time of George Washington.” The watchdog group Reinvent Albany disagrees on the grounds that satire is not what this is: “To us, it's a campaign ad meant to influence voters.” Hochul's campaign calls it “straight up lying,” and in January she said she would move to ban A.I. depictions of candidates within ninety days of an election.
Early voting Oct 24–Nov 1 · register by Oct 24 · Election Day Nov 3.

⛪The Home Wire⛪

1

Pomfret · A Firefighter Was Hurt

One firefighter sustained non-life-threatening injuries at Wednesday's blaze at the former White Village on Route 5. The cause has still not been released.

2

Falconer · Concrete Plant Burns

A commercial building housing a concrete plant is believed a total loss after a Friday afternoon fire, according to the Chautauqua County Sheriff's Office. Second major fire in the county in three days.

★The Marquee★

1

A Crowded New Music Friday

Albums from Tove Lo, Carly Rae Jepsen and beabadoobee all landed yesterday, alongside an archival David Bowie release of his Shel Talmy sessions.

2

Rhiannon Giddens Has Something to Say

The banjo player and historian released a new record and spent the week talking about A.I. in music, and about the Sheeran and Macklemore business.

3

Donna Summer, Songwriter

She was inducted posthumously into the Songwriters Hall of Fame — overdue recognition that she wrote or co-wrote most of what she sang.

🏈The Gridiron🏈

A Weekend Off, and a Game to Watch
Bills · nothing until the Chargers come to Orchard Park a week from tomorrow. Buffalo is 2–0 having won in Houston for the first time in twenty years and then put 41 on Detroit at home. The long rest after a Thursday game is the best week on any schedule.
Jets and Packers, Tomorrow at One
Jets · Green Bay at the Meadowlands, 1:00. Friday's report had Breece Hall and Kenyon Sadiq full go; Will McDonald, who put five pressures on Tennessee in twenty-five snaps, is the name to watch on the injury list. Green Bay is 0–1 and short-handed across the interior line, without Micah Parsons, and without Josh Jacobs, who is away from the team. The Packers are still favored, which is the whole story of the game.

⚑The Chase⚑

Bristol Tonight
7:30 tonight on USA, race three of ten. Half a mile of concrete banked steeper than a highway ramp; the tires give out before the drivers do, and the race usually turns on who saved rubber. Hamlin leads Larson by twelve. Larson won here in the spring.

September 19, 1982 — Scott Fahlman, a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon, proposed using :-) to mark a joke on an online message board. He suggested :-( for the other case. Both stuck.
